I can rank two variables in the same direction and average the ranks of tied values.
I can find $r_s$ on my GDC by finding $r$ for the two lists of ranks.
I can interpret $r_s$ in context, as an association between the ranks.
I can give a mathematical reason to choose $r_s$ over $r$, or $r$ over $r_s$.
I can decide whether changing one data value changes $r_s$.
Spearman's $r_s$ is Pearson's $r$ calculated on the ranks of the data instead of the values.
$r_s$ measures how monotonic a relationship is: whether $y$ always rises (or always falls) as $x$ rises, straight line or not.
Tied values share the average of the ranks they would take. Two values tied for 5th and 6th both get rank 5.5.
$r_s$ is less sensitive to outliers than $r$, because an extreme value can only move to the end of the ranking.
Changing a value without changing its rank leaves $r_s$ unchanged.
Use $r$ for a linear relationship between measurements. Use $r_s$ for ranked data, a curved but monotonic pattern, or data with outliers.
The typing data: a curved, decreasing scatter. Caption: $r=-0.899$ but $r_s=-0.994$; the pattern is monotonic, not linear.
The same scatter plotted as rank against rank. Caption: ranking straightens a monotonic pattern.
